label: Intro
title: Tagalog and the Filipino people
summary: Where the language comes from, and the culture behind it
goals: Know how Tagalog relates to Filipino and the other languages of the Philippines
Understand where many Tagalog words come from
Learn the cultural habits that shape how Tagalog is used

blocks.t: A living language is one that people use every day and that keeps changing. Tagalog is exactly that. It is the main basis of **Filipino**, the national language of the Philippines.

The 1987 Constitution says Filipino should keep growing by taking in words from other Philippine languages and from outside. That is why modern Tagalog freely mixes in Cebuano, Ilocano and English words.

blocks.title: Tagalog or Filipino?
blocks.t: In everyday life the two names are used almost interchangeably. Strictly, Tagalog is the regional language of Manila and nearby provinces, and Filipino is the national language built on it. This guide teaches the Tagalog that most Filipinos speak and understand.

head: Name
What it means
rows: Tagalog
the language of the Tagalog-speaking regions around Manila
Pilipino
the name used for the Tagalog-based national language from the 1960s
Filipino
the current name of the national language
blocks.title: Three names, one family

blocks.t: Tagalog belongs to the **Malayo-Polynesian** (also called Austronesian) family. That family stretches from Madagascar in the west to Hawaii and Easter Island in the east, so Tagalog has many distant cousins.

Long before the Spanish arrived, people in the islands wrote in a syllable-based script called **Baybayin**. Each symbol stood for a consonant plus a vowel. Today it appears mainly in art and heritage designs.

head: Source
What came from it
rows: Sanskrit and Malay
many names of plants and animals, and some abstract words
Chinese
words for trade, food, tools, family and games
Arabic
a small number of words, from early Muslim traders
Spanish
a very large number of everyday words: for religion, government, days, months, and many household things
English
modern words for technology, school and daily life, brought in under American-era education
blocks.title: Words borrowed over the centuries
Good news for English speakers
blocks.t: Because of Spanish and English loanwords, you already half know a lot of Tagalog. Lesson 1 shows how to decode them: **kompyuter** is computer and **titser** is teacher.

sections.title: How Tagalog became the national language

blocks.t: The Philippines has more than 170 languages. Eight of them (Tagalog, Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon, Bicolano, Waray, Kapampangan and Pangasinan) are spoken by about nine in ten people. They are related, but speakers of different ones often cannot understand each other.
In the 1930s, leaders chose Tagalog as the basis for a national language. The reasons were practical.

head: Reason
Why it mattered
rows: Most widely spoken and understood
more people knew it than any other Philippine language
One language, not many dialects
unlike the Visayan languages, Tagalog is fairly uniform
Rich writing
more books and poetry have been published in Tagalog than in any other local language
Language of the capital
Manila has always been the centre of government and business
Language of the Revolution
it was used by the movement for independence

blocks.t: Since then the language has been promoted in schools, radio, television, film, books and church services, and it keeps developing today.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Roughly three in ten Filipinos speak Tagalog as their first language.
About two thirds understand it to some degree, so it works almost anywhere in the country.

blocks.t: Language is easier to learn when you know the habits behind it. Filipinos are often described as warm, hospitable and family-minded, with a strong sense of humour and fairness.

head: Value
How it shows in language
rows: Respect for elders
the little word **po** and the respectful **kayo**
Concern for others
greetings that ask about your family and where you are going
Humour and warmth
friendly teasing, nicknames and lots of expressions
Flexibility
people mix English and Tagalog freely (Taglish)

blocks.title: Reading between the lines
items: A greeting like "Where are you going?" is a friendly hello, not a request for details.
A polite "yes" may sometimes mean "I heard you" rather than "I agree". Watch body language and tone.
Time is often relaxed. Being a little late is usually forgiven, but being rude is not.

blocks.title: Your goal
blocks.t: Fluency is more than grammar. Listen a lot, copy the rhythm, and use the polite forms. People respond warmly to learners who try.

exercises.q: Filipino is mainly based on which language?
exercises.explain: Filipino, the national language, is built mainly on Tagalog.

exercises.q: Tagalog belongs to which language family?
exercises.explain: It is related to languages from Madagascar to Hawaii.
Each symbol stood for a consonant plus a vowel.

exercises.q: Which language gave Tagalog the largest number of everyday loanwords?
exercises.explain: Days, months, and many household words come from Spanish.

exercises.q: Why was Tagalog chosen as the base of the national language?
options: It was widely spoken and the language of the capital
It was the oldest language in the world
It had no dialects at all
exercises.answer: It was widely spoken and the language of the capital
exercises.explain: It was the most widely spoken and understood, with rich writing.

exercises.q: "Saan ka pupunta?" (Where are you going?) is often meant as…
exercises.explain: Filipinos often greet with questions about where you are going.

exercises.q: Which little word shows respect to older people?
Match each word to its meaning.

recap: Tagalog is the base of Filipino, the national language.
It belongs to the Malayo-Polynesian family and has borrowed from Sanskrit, Malay, Chinese, Arabic, Spanish and English.
Tagalog was chosen because it was widely spoken, uniform, rich in literature, and the language of Manila.
Respect, warmth and family come through in the language, especially in po and greetings.
